newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's government to go it alone on budget.
newsitem.headline: Italy's government to go it alone on budget.

text.p: Silvio Berlusconi's Freedom Alliance bloc rejected a move to resolve a bitter stand-off over the 1997 budget on Tuesday and the government said it would now go it alone with the controversial austerity package.

The centre-right Freedom Alliance has demanded that Prime Minister Romano Prodi drop plans to introduce fiscal reform in the budget and on Monday announced that it would no longer attend parliamentary debate on the package in protest.

In a bid to defuse the row, Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco on Tuesday provided more details of the tax overhaul, but still asked for the government to be given special powers to work out the small print without having to return to parliament again.
The Freedom Alliance said in a statement they were being told too little too late and accused Prodi of wanting to impose the government's policies on the country.
"The government wants parliament to decide in the space of two days a fiscal reform which is destined to condition the future of the country for many years to come," it said.

The lower house of parliament has to approve the budget, which aims to slash a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) off next year's deficit, by November 14. It will then pass to the Senate (Upper House) for ratification.
Prodi's centre-left coalition condemned the Freedom Alliance's budget boycott and said they would now pass the bill into law by themselves.

"They have said 'no' to our every offer. It's an unprecedented breakdown," said Fabio Mussi, parliamentary party leader of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) -- the largest party within the coalition.

The government, which controls the lower house thanks to external support from the hardline Communist Refoundation Party, should have no problem voting through the budget, but the opposition walkout will challenge the legitimacy of the vote.
The package, which Prodi has said is crucial if Italy is to become a founder member of Europe's planned single currency, includes a one-off Euro tax and is hugely unpopular.

More than half a million people marched through Rome at the weekend to protest against the bill, sending a shiver through the six-month old coalition and spurring the opposition to announce their parliamentary walkout.
The boycott has also generated strains within the government, with coalition parties increasingly worried about the power the Communist Refoundation now wield.
Without the opposition, Refoundation now ensures the legal quorum in the lower house and can halt debate at any moment.

The party is opposed to any attempt by Prodi to seek a compromise with Berlusconi and in a show of power on Monday night, it briefly withdrew from parliament on word that behind-the-scenes talks were going on.

The muscle-flexing drew howls of protest from coalition parties. "Don't they realise this is political suicide," said Lanfranco Turci, a senior member of the largest coalition partner, the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS).
"They have an atomic bomb and insist on always using it."
